items.prompt: What's the key difference between the formal org chart and the informal decision network?
choices: They're described as always being identical in any organization that's genuinely well run
The formal chart shows who reports to whom; the informal network shows who a decision-maker actually consults or trusts before making a call
The informal network is described as being flatly illegal for anyone to actually use
The formal chart is described as simply being more accurate, since it's the one that's documented
items.explanation: These are genuinely different things — reporting structure versus who actually shapes a decision-maker's thinking — and conflating them is exactly what caused the CI proposal to stall.
items.reference:
Formal chartInformal network
ShowsWho reports to whomWho's actually consulted/trusted

Why: both are real, but only one was where the CI decision actually got made.
items.learnMore:
Two real, different structures

Neither chart is 'the fake one' — they answer genuinely different questions, and knowing which one governs a given decision is the actual skill.

Common mistake

Assuming the formal chart is always the operative one for every kind of decision.

items.prompt: Is the existence of an informal decision network, decoupled from title, a flaw in how the organization runs?

No — it's a natural consequence of trust being built through repeated demonstrated judgment, which an org chart can't encode
Yes, and it's described as something that should be actively eliminated through better documentation
It's a flaw, but one described as simply unavoidable in any sufficiently large company
items.explanation: The unit frames this as a natural, expected consequence of how trust actually forms — through years of reliable judgment — not a design flaw to be fixed.
items.reference:
A director trusts the senior IC because of years of reliably good judgment — not anything an org chart could encode.

Why: trust is built through interaction, not assigned by title.
items.learnMore:
Trust isn't assignable

No org chart update can manufacture the kind of trust that comes from years of a decision-maker seeing someone's judgment proven reliable — this is why the informal network exists in every organization, not just poorly-run ones.

Common mistake

Treating the informal network as evidence of organizational dysfunction rather than a normal feature of how trust works.

items.prompt: Does a proposal stalling in the formal channel mean the proposal itself was flawed?
choices: Yes — the formal channel is described as existing specifically to catch flawed proposals
Not necessarily — it can mean the formal channel was never where this category of decision actually got evaluated in this org
Yes, always, without exception, regardless of what the actual evaluation process looked like
No — stalled proposals are described as always eventually getting approved regardless of merit
items.explanation: The unit distinguishes between 'the proposal is wrong' and 'the proposal never reached genuine evaluation' — the CI proposal's stall was an example of the latter.
items.reference:
Path A's proposal wasn't wrong — it had no upstream evaluation step in an org where that step usually happens informally first.

Why: a stalled proposal in the formal queue often means it was never actually evaluated, not that it was rejected.
items.learnMore:
Stalled ≠ rejected

A proposal sitting unread in a queue and a proposal that was carefully evaluated and turned down are very different situations that can look identical from outside — distinguishing them matters for what to do next.

Common mistake

Concluding a stalled proposal was judged and found wanting, when it may never have been genuinely evaluated at all.

items.prompt: What does this unit say the practical skill of reading the informal network is FOR?

Currying favor with anyone who happens to be influential, regardless of actual merit
Deliberately undermining people who hold formal authority within the organization
items.explanation: The stated purpose is accurate understanding of how decisions actually happen — not bypassing legitimate process, and not currying favor independent of merit.
items.reference:
Knowing where a decision genuinely gets made is what separates "I did everything right and it went nowhere" from getting things done.

Why: this is about accurate understanding, not bypassing legitimate process.

Understanding, not circumventing

items.prompt: What are the four observable signals L2 uses to spot real influence?
choices: A person's salary, their tenure at the company, their title, and their total headcount

Whoever happens to be most frequently praised by name in public company-wide channels
items.explanation: These four signals — being looped in, being cited, attending without chairing, and disagreement having outsized weight — together reveal real influence, unlike any formal metric.
items.reference:
1. Looped in without a formal role 2. Cited when explaining WHY

3. In every meeting, chairs none 4. Disagreement alone can stall a decision

Why: convergence of multiple signals on the same person is what makes the informal network legible.
items.learnMore:
Signals, not proof

No single signal alone is conclusive — it's the convergence of multiple signals on the same person, across otherwise unrelated situations, that makes the identification reliable.

Common mistake

Concluding real influence from a single observed signal rather than looking for convergence across several.

items.prompt: Why does L3 suggest periodically re-running the "trace the last three decisions" exercise, rather than doing it once?
choices: Because the exercise is described as only ever being accurate the very first time it's run
Because the informal network shifts over time as people join, leave, or change roles, so a one-time diagnosis can go stale
Because it's described as needing to be carried out differently each time for legal reasons
There's described as being no real reason at all — repetition is said to add no real value
items.explanation: The network's membership isn't fixed — it changes as relationships and roles change, which is exactly why L3 frames re-observation as necessary maintenance, not a one-time task.
items.reference:
The informal network is a living structure, not a fixed map you learn once.

Why: the specific relationship changes; the skill of observing current patterns doesn't.
items.learnMore:
A living structure

Treating the informal network as something learned once and never revisited is a real, common mistake — people join, leave, and change roles, and the network shifts accordingly.

Common mistake

Treating an outdated understanding of the informal network as still accurate after significant personnel changes.

items.prompt: L3's second extension asks: what if there's no clear informal influencer for a category of decision at all? What does it suggest?
choices: This exact situation is described as being impossible in any real organization at all
The formal channel may genuinely be the only real evaluation step, so the fix is making the formal proposal itself excellent enough to be self-evidently worth prioritizing
Wait patiently until an informal influencer eventually emerges before proposing anything at all
Escalate the matter directly to the CEO whenever this exact situation comes up
items.explanation: L3 acknowledges this case explicitly — in a flat or young org with no established informal trust relationships yet, the formal channel may genuinely be the only real path, requiring a different approach: a stronger self-contained proposal.
items.reference:
No clear informal influencer → the formal channel may be the ONLY real evaluation step → make the proposal self-evidently strong

Why: not every org has an established informal network for every category of decision yet.
items.learnMore:
When there's no informal shortcut

A flat or newly-formed org may genuinely lack the kind of established trust relationships this unit describes — recognizing this and adjusting strategy accordingly is itself part of reading the org accurately.

Common mistake

Assuming an informal influencer must exist somewhere and searching indefinitely rather than recognizing the formal channel may genuinely be the only real path.

items.prompt: Why might a flat or very new organization lack a clear informal decision network for some categories of decisions?
choices: Because flat organizations of this kind are described as being inherently dysfunctional overall
Because the informal network is built through years of demonstrated trust, which simply hasn't had time to form yet in a young or flat structure
Because informal networks of this kind are described as only ever existing in large companies
Flat organizations are described as always having MORE informal influence overall, not less
items.explanation: Since the informal network requires time and repeated interaction to form (per L1's core point), a young or flat org may genuinely not have had time to develop one yet for certain kinds of decisions.
items.reference:

items.prompt: Per L3's failure-modes table, what's wrong with treating "loop in the influential person" as a way to skip formal approval entirely?
choices: Nothing at all is described as being wrong with this — it's framed as the recommended shortcut
Path B still required the director's sign-off — the informal step supplemented the formal one, it never replaced it
This is described as only ever being a problem for employees who are relatively junior
Skipping formal approval entirely is described as always being fine, as long as the idea is good enough
items.explanation: This is explicitly listed as a failure mode — misunderstanding the relationship between informal evaluation and formal approval as substitution rather than sequence.
items.reference:
Failure modeWhat it gets wrong
Treating informal loop-in as skipping formal approvalPath B still required sign-off — informal supplements formal, doesn't replace it

Why: this misunderstanding could lead to genuinely bypassing legitimate process, which this unit doesn't endorse.
items.learnMore:
Supplement, not substitute

Every worked example in this unit keeps the formal approval step intact — the informal evaluation only ever changes how quickly and confidently the formal step happens, never whether it happens.

Common mistake

Believing a strong informal endorsement means formal sign-off can be treated as a formality to skip.

items.prompt: Per L3's failure-modes table, what's wrong with currying favor with influential people regardless of whether the underlying case has merit?
choices: Nothing at all — this is described as being the actual core strategy that the unit teaches
The senior IC's endorsement mattered because their judgment is reliable, not because they're simply well-connected — merit-free favor-currying misses the actual mechanism
It's described as only being a problem at all if the influential person in question happens to notice
This particular approach is described as always working out better than simply having a strong case
items.explanation: The unit is explicit that the IC's endorsement carried weight BECAUSE of their reliable judgment on real merit — courting influence without merit misunderstands why the mechanism worked in the first place.

items.prompt: A proposal has genuine merit but the proposer skips getting feedback from anyone in the informal network before submitting it formally. What's the risk, per L2?
choices: There's described as being no real risk at all — formal submission alone is described as always sufficient

In an org where a real evaluation step happens informally first, the proposal may land in a formal queue without the pre-vetting decision-makers have learned to expect, risking the same stall as Path A
The proposal is described as being automatically rejected outright, with no further consideration given
This is described as always being the correct approach to take, regardless of the org's own decision patterns
items.explanation: This is essentially Path A's situation — a sound proposal that skips the informal evaluation step an org may implicitly expect, risking the same kind of stall even though the underlying idea is good.
items.reference:
Legitimate: get feedback early from real decision-shapers on a sound proposal

Not this: currying favor regardless of merit, or routing around formal approval

Why: the map itself is neutral — how it's used is what matters.
items.learnMore:
The map is neutral

The same accurate map of who holds influence can be used well or poorly — the map itself doesn't determine which, the proposal's merit and respect for formal process do.

Common mistake

Treating knowledge of the informal network as inherently manipulative, rather than neutral information that can be used well or poorly.

items.prompt: Why does L2 look for CONVERGENCE across multiple signals, rather than relying on just one, like being cc'd on a thread?
choices: Convergence isn't actually described as necessary at all — a single signal is said to always be sufficient

Being cc'd once could be incidental; convergence across several independent signals (loop-in, citation, meeting presence, disagreement weight) is much stronger evidence of a genuine influence relationship
Multiple signals are described as being required purely because of a formal company policy
Convergence of this kind is described as being essentially impossible to observe in practice
items.explanation: A single signal could have an innocent, unrelated explanation; multiple independent signals converging on the same person is what makes the identification reliable rather than a guess.
items.reference:
1. Looped in without a formal role 2. Cited when explaining WHY

3. In every meeting, chairs none 4. Disagreement alone can stall a decision

Why: convergence of multiple signals on the same person is what makes the informal network legible.
items.learnMore:
Signals, not proof

No single signal alone is conclusive — it's the convergence of multiple signals on the same person, across otherwise unrelated situations, that makes the identification reliable.

Common mistake

Concluding real influence from a single observed signal rather than looking for convergence across several.

items.prompt: Was the new engineer's original proposal in Path A factually or technically wrong?
choices: Yes — the proposal's own technical flaws are described as being exactly why it stalled in the queue
No — L3 never suggests the proposal itself was flawed; it stalled due to a missing upstream evaluation step, not a technical problem
It's described as being genuinely unclear whether the original proposal was technically sound at all
The proposal is described as having actually been wrong, right up until the IC's edge case was identified
items.explanation: The proposal was not wrong in its core idea. L3 does show the IC found an edge case, so the proposal could be improved, but the reason Path A stalled was structural: it lacked trusted upstream evaluation.
items.reference:
Path APath B
Formal approval requiredYesYes (same step, same director)

Why: the gap wasn't process, it was the presence or absence of an upstream evaluation.
items.learnMore:
Same formal step, different upstream reality

This table makes the comparison concrete — both paths required identical formal approval; only the presence of a trusted upstream evaluator differed.

Common mistake

Assuming Path B 'went around' the director rather than reaching the same approval faster because of an added evaluation step.

items.prompt: If a new person emerges as the trusted informal evaluator for infrastructure decisions after the original IC leaves, would this new person necessarily hold influence in exactly the same shape as the original IC?
choices: Yes, always — the role itself is described as being fixed and gets filled identically each and every time
Not necessarily — L3 notes it could be a different shape entirely (e.g. a working group instead of one person), which is why re-observation matters rather than assuming a like-for-like replacement
No — it's described as being the case that no one can ever truly replace an established informal influencer
The shape that influence takes is described as being irrelevant to how proposals should actually be approached
items.explanation: L3 explicitly notes the replacement could take a different shape (like a working group) rather than a single person — reinforcing why re-running the observation exercise matters rather than assuming a direct substitute.

items.prompt: In an org with no established informal influencer for a decision category, what should the proposal itself compensate for?
choices: Nothing in particular — the proposal is described as needing to be written exactly the same regardless of context
The absence of a pre-vetting step — the proposal needs to be self-evidently strong enough to be prioritized without an informal endorsement carrying it
The proposal should instead be made deliberately vague, specifically in order to avoid any real scrutiny
The proposer should instead go out and artificially recruit an informal influencer before submitting anything
items.explanation: Without an informal pre-vetting step available, the formal proposal has to do all the persuasive work on its own — this is the adjustment L3 suggests for orgs where no informal network exists yet for that decision type.
items.reference:
No clear informal influencer → the formal channel may be the ONLY real evaluation step → make the proposal self-evidently strong

Why: not every org has an established informal network for every category of decision yet.
